notes.meaning: Jerusalem's former beauty has faded away under God's righteous judgment. The shining treasures of the temple, and the holy people who served there, now lie ruined and tossed into the city streets. What was once precious to God has been treated like common rubble.

The people and leaders of Zion were once valued like fine gold. After the city was conquered, the Babylonians treated them like cheap clay pots. They were smashed and tossed aside as though they had no worth at all.

Wild animals like jackals still nurse and care for their young. In the terrible famine during the siege, starving mothers could not provide milk for their babies. They seemed as uncaring as ostriches that leave their eggs in the open dirt.

Babies in Jerusalem suffered terribly because their mothers had no milk to give them. Their tongues stuck to the roofs of their mouths from severe thirst. Older children cried out and begged for bread, but nobody had any food left to share.

People who grew up eating fine food collapsed hungry in the streets. Wealthy citizens who once wore rich scarlet clothes were reduced to sitting on filthy ash heaps and garbage piles. They clung to those trash piles just to rest or search for scraps of food.

Jerusalem's suffering became worse than the destruction of Sodom. Sodom was wiped out in a single moment by fire from heaven without a long struggle. Jerusalem had to endure months of agonizing starvation, pain, and enemy attacks.

Jerusalem's leaders and dedicated men were once healthy, radiant, and strong. Their clear skin and bright appearance showed how richly God had blessed them. They stood out like dazzling snow and polished gems.

The brutal famine changed their looks completely. Starvation made their faces dark and sunken, so that their own neighbors no longer recognized them in the street. Their flesh wasted away, leaving dry skin clinging to their bones like withered wood.

Dying quickly in battle was better than starving slowly inside the city walls. Soldiers struck down by the sword were put out of their misery right away. Those suffering from famine slowly wasted away in agony because the fields had no food.

Mothers who were normally tender and caring were driven to horrible extremes by hunger. With no food left, they boiled and ate their own children to stay alive. The long siege broke down natural affection and filled the city with horror.

The Lord fully poured out the fierce anger He had warned about. He sent judgment that acted like a blazing fire against Zion. That fire did not stop at the surface, but burned down the city to its very foundations.

Foreign kings and nations never expected Jerusalem to fall to an enemy. The city was protected by high walls and had often been guarded by God's own power. Its total defeat proved that God Himself had decided to hand it over to the Babylonians.

This terrible destruction fell upon the city because its spiritual guides had become corrupt. The false prophets and wicked priests misled the people and killed righteous servants of God. Their bloodguilt brought the nation to ruin.

These guilty leaders wandered through the streets like blind men in a daze. Their hands and robes were so stained with the blood of the innocent that they were completely defiled. Other people avoided them so they would not be made unclean.

People shouted at these bloody leaders to get away, just as they would warn others away from lepers. When the disgraced leaders fled into exile, even foreign nations did not want them around. The wicked teachers found nowhere to rest in peace.

The Lord Himself scattered these ungodly leaders in His anger and turned His care away from them. When the Babylonian conquerors arrived, they showed no mercy to the aged and gave no special honor to the priests.

The people of Judah wore themselves out watching for an ally to rescue them. They put their trust in Egypt instead of turning back to the Lord. In the end, that foreign nation was unable to save them from Babylon.
The Babylonians surrounded the city and hunted down anyone who moved, making the streets completely unsafe. The citizens knew that their time had run out and their nation was doomed.
The Babylonian soldiers moved faster than eagles diving for prey. They chased the fleeing people across the mountains and set traps for them in the wilderness. There was nowhere left to run or hide.

King Zedekiah, the Lord's anointed ruler from the line of David, was trapped and captured while trying to escape. The people had hoped his rule would shelter them and keep their nation alive among foreign powers. When he fell into the enemy's hands, their last earthly hope was crushed.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Traditional Latin translations render the title as 'Christ the Lord' taken in our sins, seeing the verse as pointing directly to Jesus Christ.

notes.meaning: The prophet speaks with bitter irony to Edom, telling them to enjoy their moment of celebration. Edom had gloated over Jerusalem's fall, but the cup of God's judgment was coming their way too. Soon they would be overwhelmed with shame and ruin.

Jerusalem is comforted with the promise that her period of punishment is coming to an end. God will not leave His people in exile forever. At the same time, Edom will be called to account, and all her cruel deeds will be uncovered and punished.

differ.view: Some view Zion's completed punishment as a picture of the cross, where Christ bore the full penalty for believers so that God demands no further payment from them.
